lessons.title: Reading a Cash Flow Statement Without an Accounting Degree

children.text: Every Indian company of any size prepares a cash flow statement, and almost nobody outside the finance team reads it. That is a wasted opportunity, because it is the one statement that cannot be dressed up easily. It starts from profit, strips out everything that was not cash, and ends at the change in the bank balance. This lesson walks through a complete statement line by line, in plain language, so you can pick up your own company's annual report and follow it.

body.text: The cash flow statement is a bridge. It starts at profit, which is an accounting opinion, and ends at the bank balance, which is a fact. Everything in between explains the difference.

children.text: Why It Starts From Profit and Works Backwards
There are two ways to present operating cash flow. The
direct method
lists actual receipts and payments. The
indirect method
starts at profit and adjusts it.

markDefs.definition: Lists actual cash receipts from customers and cash paid to suppliers and employees. Simple to read, but few Indian companies publish it because it needs a separate cash-basis record.
Starts from profit before tax and adjusts for non-cash items and working capital changes to arrive at operating cash flow. This is what you will see in almost every Indian annual report.

children.text: In practice, every annual report you pick up from an NSE or BSE listed company will use the indirect method. So that is the format worth learning. It has three blocks, in a fixed order, always.

body.title: Two ways to present the same number

columns.label: Direct method
points: Cash received from customers, less cash paid to suppliers and staff
Tells you nothing about why cash differs from profit

columns.label: Indirect method
points: Profit before tax, adjusted for non-cash items and working capital
Used by almost every Indian company
Shows exactly where the profit leaked away

body.text: That last line is the honesty check. The closing cash figure has to match the cash and bank balance on the balance sheet exactly. Profit can be debated. A bank balance cannot.

body.title: Why is interest added back and then subtracted again?

children.text: It looks like an accounting trick, but it has a purpose. Interest is a financing cost, not an operating one. Two companies running identical factories should show the same operating cash flow even if one is debt-free and the other is loaded with loans.
Profit before tax already had ₹9 crore of interest deducted from it.
The statement adds that ₹9 crore back, so operating cash flow reflects the business alone, with no borrowing decisions in it.
The same ₹9 crore then appears as a real cash payment under financing, where it belongs.
The net effect on total cash is zero. What you gain is a clean operating number you can compare across companies and across years.

body.title: Build the operating line yourself
body.prompt: A company reports profit before tax of ₹60 crore, depreciation of ₹25 crore and finance costs of ₹8 crore. Receivables rose by ₹20 crore, inventory fell by ₹5 crore, payables rose by ₹4 crore, and it paid ₹16 crore of income tax. There is no interest income. What is its net cash from operating activities, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 60 plus 25 plus 8 gives ₹93 crore before working capital. Working capital: minus 20 for higher receivables, plus 5 because inventory fell and released cash, plus 4 for higher payables, a net minus ₹11 crore. That gives ₹82 crore generated from operations, less ₹16 crore of tax paid, so ₹66 crore. Note that a fall in inventory adds cash, while a rise consumes it.

body.title: Why the add-back exists
body.textWithBlank: Depreciation is added back to profit in the cash flow statement because it is a ___ expense.
body.explanation: The cash for that asset left the bank in the year it was bought, and appeared then as an investing outflow. Charging depreciation later reduces profit without any further cash leaving, so it is added back.

children.text: Reading the Three Signs Together
Once you can find the three subtotals, you can diagnose a business in about thirty seconds. It is the pattern of plus and minus signs that tells the story, not the individual numbers.

body.caption: What the sign pattern usually means

cells: Mature and self-funding. Operations pay for growth and still repay lenders. Sahyadri Foods sits here
Growing fast. Operations generate cash, but expansion is large enough to need borrowing too
Early stage or in trouble. Everything is funded by lenders or investors. Fine for a funded startup, alarming for a 20-year-old manufacturer
Shrinking or selling assets. Check whether the positive investing line is a genuine strategic exit or distress selling

body.text: One weak year proves nothing. Working capital swings, a delayed government receipt or one large advance can distort a single year badly. Always read at least three to five years together before judging a company.

children.text: A Real Company: Asian Paints
Here is the same comparison for a company everyone knows. These are consolidated figures from screener.in for the five years ended March 2026, in ₹ crore.

body.title: Asian Paints: net profit vs operating cash flow (₹ crore)

children.text: Look at the year to March 2022. Asian Paints earned ₹3,085 crore of net profit and generated only ₹986 crore of operating cash, less than a third of it. That is exactly the working capital effect from Lesson 1.1, at the scale of a large listed company. Now look at the five years together: ₹20,943 crore of cumulative profit against ₹22,795 crore of cumulative operating cash, about 1.09 times. Over a full cycle, a strong business converts its profit into cash.

body.text: This is the habit worth building. Never judge cash conversion from one year. Add up five years of net profit, add up five years of operating cash flow, and compare the totals. One bad year is weather. Five bad years is a business model.

body.label: screener.in company page
body.description: Scroll to the Cash Flows section for ten years of operating, investing and financing figures on any NSE or BSE listed company.

body.title: Spot the odd line
body.question: Which of these would NOT appear under operating activities in an Indian cash flow statement?
options: Income tax paid during the year
body.explanation: Loan principal repayment is a financing activity. Tax paid, working capital movements and non-cash add-backs all sit in the operating block. This matters in practice: a company can show strong operating cash flow and still be struggling, because the principal repayments that drain it are reported further down.

body.title: The subsidiary that looks fine on paper
body.scenario: You are a business head reviewing a small subsidiary. Its profit and loss statement shows ₹8 crore of profit before tax, up from ₹5 crore last year. The cash flow statement shows operating cash flow of ₹1 crore, down from ₹4 crore. Receivables rose by ₹6 crore, inventory is flat, and financing shows ₹7 crore of fresh borrowing. The unit head opens the review by calling it a record year.
body.prompt: What do you ask, and in what order?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Who owes the ₹6 crore? Ask for a receivables ageing list by customer. A jump this size is usually one or two accounts, not a general trend.
2. How much of it is overdue beyond agreed terms, and what has actually been collected since the year end?
3. Did we change credit terms or push sales at the year end to hit a target? Revenue billed in the last week of March is profit this year and cash next year, if at all.
4. Are any of these customers disputing invoices or waiting on a delivery sign-off?
5. What is the ₹7 crore of new borrowing funding, and at what interest rate? Profit that exists only as receivables is being financed by the lender, and the interest is real cash.
6. What would the same statement look like if we collected on time? That is the target, and the collections plan should be owned by name, with weekly follow-up.
The record year may well be genuine. But profit up ₹3 crore while operating cash falls ₹3 crore means the growth is currently sitting in someone else's bank account.

body.title: Read your own company's statement in ten minutes
steps: Find the cash flow statement in the latest annual report, or on screener.in if the company is listed.
Write down the three subtotals: operating, investing and financing.
Check the sign pattern against the table above and decide which story fits.
Compare operating cash flow with net profit for the same year, and then for the last five years added together.
In the operating block, find the receivables and inventory lines. These are usually the biggest leaks.
In the financing block, add up principal repaid plus interest paid. That is the fixed cash the business must produce every year before anything else.
Confirm the closing cash figure matches the cash and bank line on the balance sheet.

cards.definition: Starts from profit before tax and adjusts for non-cash items and working capital to reach operating cash flow.

cards.term: Operating profit before working capital changes
cards.definition: Profit rebuilt on a cash basis, before any balance sheet movement is counted.
The figure after working capital changes but before tax paid.
Cash generated from operations less income tax actually paid. The health check of the core business.
Operating cash flow less capital expenditure. What is genuinely available for lenders and owners.
Operating cash flow divided by net profit. Read it over five years, never one.

points: The cash flow statement bridges profit and the bank balance, and its closing figure must tie to the balance sheet.
Indian companies use the indirect method: start at profit before tax, add back non-cash items, adjust working capital, then deduct tax paid.
Rising receivables and inventory consume cash. Rising payables retain it.
Interest is added back in operating and shown again in financing, so operating cash flow is comparable across companies with different debt.
The pattern of plus and minus signs across the three blocks diagnoses a business faster than any single number.
Asian Paints converted only about a third of its March 2022 profit into operating cash, yet about 1.09 times over five years. Always read the cycle, not the year.

body.text: Sahyadri Foods Limited is fictional. The Asian Paints figures are consolidated data from screener.in as published at the time of writing and may be restated or updated later. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
